catalog_quote: 2.4.2 Stress Stress is not phonemic and much of the language is mono-syllabic anyway. In general, the final syllable is stressed, with these provisos: (a) Dialect variation: Although only brief word lists have been taken in other dialects, there seems to be a tendency in the Eastern dialects for stress to occur on first syllables. (b) Suffixed or compound words: The stress is normally retained on the final syllable before suffixation, for example the post-positional clitic ŋga ‘of/for’ is very common. When added to a word, stress does not pass to it: (11) tu di'naŋ + -ŋga —› tu di'naŋ-ŋga ‘because of that’ (12) a'maŋ + daŋ —› a'maŋdaŋ ‘five’ (lit. ‘one hand’) (13) dô'mbwê + ŋa'kwa —› dô'mbwêkwa ‘spine, backbone’ (c) Emphasis: exclamations are often stressed on the first syllable. For example: (14) na'whê ‘wife’ cf. 'nawhê ‘(call or summons to) wife’

new_statements.rule_in_words: Bukawa is a tone language (contrastive high vs low tone, lexically unpredictable, section 2.4.1); stress is separately described as non-phonemic and falling on the final syllable of the (simple, mostly mono- or disyllabic) word. Clitics/suffixes and the second member of most compounds do not attract stress, so stress stays on the final syllable of the base/first morpheme; emphatic/vocative exclamations may shift stress to the first syllable; Eastern dialects reportedly tend toward initial stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing on secondary stress; p.120 notes each word in a complex predicate carries a single primary stress (used as evidence of wordhood).
new_statements.exceptions: Eastern dialects tend to initial stress (based on brief word lists only); clitic -ŋga and compound second members unstressed (a'maŋ+daŋ -> a'maŋdaŋ 'five', dô'wa+a'whê -> dô'wawê), but compounds with lau 'people' keep final stress (lau'whê 'women', lau'ŋgac 'men', p.18); exclamations stressed on first syllable ('nawhê vocative vs na'whê 'wife'). Author also speculates (p.14) that glottal stop is usually preceded by high tone, 'This may also be linked with stress', and that tone may interact with intonation 'and perhaps even stress'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress on simple (citation) words; morphological base rather than the suffixed/compounded phonological word is the domain (stress does not move onto clitics or compound second members). Language is described as tonal (register tone, high/low), with stress explicitly non-phonemic; the reading 'fixed: final syllable' is the stress rule, and a 'tone language with a stress statement' flag also applies.
new_statements.identity_note: Eckermann 2007 describes Bukawa (Bugawac, ISO buk, glottocode buga1250) as spoken on the north Huon Gulf coast, Morobe Province; the description is based mainly on the central/western (Bukawa village / Cape Arkona area) dialect, and the author notes that Eastern dialects (brief word lists only) tend toward first-syllable stress instead of final stress. The book's file name spells the author 'Eckerman'; title page has 'Eckermann'.
